claims.text: The creep resistance of the dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating is governed by the stability of its dual-phase interfaces.
The BCC phase acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Mesoscopic chemical order is retained under sustained stress.
Interfacial pinning slows progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
The as-deposited coating has interconnected FCC and BCC regions.
The initial coating contains mesoscopic chemical-ordering domains.
Continuous elevated-temperature creep loading is representative of the coating's service conditions.
The creep tests will be conducted under constant high stress and high temperature within the coating's operating bounds.
FCC/BCC interfaces and associated chemical-order domains resist dislocation nucleation and glide.
The BCC phase has coherent interfaces with the FCC phase.
BCC regions and coherent FCC/BCC interfaces impede dislocation motion and delay plastic flow during continuous loading.
The dual-phase configuration promotes grain-boundary and phase-boundary pinning.
Boundary pinning reduces creep rate relative to samples in which continuous loading disrupts the interfaces or chemical-order domains.
Samples that maintain intact FCC/BCC interfaces will exhibit a significantly lower creep rate.
Samples that maintain intact interfaces will show slower deformation kinetics and less microstructural degradation over time.
At extreme temperatures, phase instability may cause the proposed interface-controlled creep-resistance mechanism to fail.
Electrical resistivity and hardness can be used to assess deformation-associated changes in mesoscopic chemical domains.
The hypothesis is refuted if interface-disrupted samples have creep rates similar to or lower than interface-intact samples, or if interface stability does not correlate with creep resistance.
